chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from Muhammad ibn Isa, from Yunus, and from his father, from Ibn Fazzal, all together, from Abu Al-Hasan Al-Rida (peace be upon him), who said:
Yunus said: 'I presented the book to him, and he said: It is correct.'

And Ibn Fazzal said: 'Amir Al-Mu'minin (peace be upon him) judged: When a man is injured in one of his eyes, it is measured with an egg tied over the injured eye, and the vision of the healthy eye is observed to see where it ends. Then the healthy eye is covered, and the vision of the injured eye is observed to see where it ends. He is given his blood money (diyah) based on this calculation, and the compurgation (qasamah/oath-swearing) along with it is from the six parts, according to the extent of the injury to his eye.'

If it was a sixth of his vision, he alone swears and is given; if it was a third, he swears and another man swears with him; if it was half, he swears and two men swear with him; if it was two-thirds, he swears and three persons swear with him; if it was four-fifths, he swears and four persons swear with him; if it was all his vision, he swears and five persons swear with him. And thus is the compurgation in all cases regarding injuries.

And if there is no one for the injured person to swear with, the oaths are doubled upon him. If it was a sixth of his vision, he swears once; if it was a third, he swears twice; and if it is more, it is according to this calculation. And indeed, the compurgation is based on the extent of his vision.

And if it is hearing, it is upon a similar manner, except that something is struck for him until the extent of his hearing is known. Then that is measured, and the compurgation is according to what is lacking from his hearing. If his hearing was complete, and mischief is feared from him, he is left until he sleeps a little, then he is shouted at. If he hears, the judge judges between them by his opinion.

And if the deficiency is in the upper arm or thigh, the measure of that is known. His healthy leg is measured with a cord, then his injured leg is measured, so the measure of what his leg or hand has lost is known. If the shin or forearm is injured, it is measured from the thigh and upper arm, and the judge looks at the measure of his thigh.

A number of our companions, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Al-Hasan ibn Zareef, from his father Zareef ibn Nasih, from a man called Abdullah ibn Ayoub, who said: 'Abu Amr Al-Mutatabbib told me: I presented this book to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him).'

And Ali ibn Fazzal, from Al-Hasan ibn Al-Jahm, who said: 'I presented it to Abu Al-Hasan Al-Rida (peace be upon him), and he said to me: Report it, for it is correct.' Then he mentioned similar to it.

key_terms.دِيَة: Blood money / compensation for injury or death
key_terms.قَسَامَة: Compurgation / oath-swearing by a group to establish a claim

ai.seo_question: How is the extent of eye injury measured to determine blood money and oath-swearing in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith, transmitted through multiple chains including direct verification by Imam al-Rida (AS), outlines the precise forensic methodology for assessing partial injuries to the eyes, ears, and limbs to calculate blood money (diyah) and the number of oath-swears (qasamah). It highlights the Shia scholarly emphasis on empirical measurement—such as using an egg or thread to compare healthy and injured limbs—ensuring equitable compensation based on the actual degree of functional loss rather than fixed categories.

en.hubeali:
Ali Bin Ibrahim, from Muhammad Bin Isa, from Yunus, and from his father, from Ibn Fazzal both together,
(It has been narrated) from Abu Al-Hassan Al-Reza<sup>asws</sup>.
Yunus said, ‘I presented the book to him<sup>asws</sup>, so he<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘It is correct’.

And Ibn Fazal said, ‘Amir Al-Momineen<sup>asws</sup> judged: ‘When the man is hit in one of his eyes, so it would be measured by an egg. The hit eye would be covered, and he would look what his correct eye can end up visualising. Then his correct eye would be covered, and he would look at what his hit eye can end up (visualising). So he would be given a wergild based upon that accounting. And the sworn endorsement along with that are from six parts, upon a measurement of what he has been hit from his eye.

So if it was such that a sixth of his vision had gone so he alone would have to swear an oath and he would be given; and if it was that a third of his vision had gone, he and another man along with him would have to swear an oath; and if it was that half of his vision had gone, he and two men along with him would swear an oath; and if it was that two-thirds of his vision had gone, he and three persons would swear an oath; and if it was that four-fifths of his vision had gone, he and four persons would have to swear an oath along with him; and if it was that all of it is gone, he and five persons along with him would have to swear an oath. And similar to that are the sworn endorsements, all of these regarding the injuries.

And if there does not happen to be for the one whose eyesight was hit, anyone who would swear an oath along with him, the swearing would be additional upon him. If it was such that a sixth of his vision had gone, he would swear once; and if it was such that a third of his vision had gone, he would have to swear twice; and if it was more, it would be upon this counting. But rather, the sworn endorsements (compurgation) are upon to what extent his vision reaches.

And if it was the hearing, so it would be approximate from that, apart from that something would be struck (to make a sound) to him, until the extent of his hearing is known. Then that would be compared, and the sworn endorsement would be approximated based upon what his hearing had been measured. So if it was such that all of his hearing (was lost), and mischief was feared from him, so he would be left to sleep until when he had slept a little, he would be shrieked at. So if he were to hear, the judge would compare between them by his opinion.

And if it was such that the deficiency was regarding the upper arms and the thighs, so that would be known by comparing the healthy leg by a cord. Then his hit leg would be compared. Thus it would be known, the measurement of the deficiency of his leg, or his hand. So if the injury was to the leg or the arm, so it is from (the measuring device) for the thigh and the upper arm that he would be compared, and the judge would look at the measurement of his thigh’.
A number of our companions, from Sahl Bin Ziyad, from Al Hassan Bin Zareyf, from his father Zareyf Bin Nasih, from a man caled Abdullah Bin Ayoub,

(It has been narrated) from Abu Amro Al Mutatabbab who said, ‘I presented the book to Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup>’.
And Ali Bin Fazzal, from Al Hassan Bin Al Jahm who said,
‘I presented it to Abu Al-Hassan Al-Reza<sup>asws</sup>, so he<sup>asws</sup> said to me: ‘Report it, for it is correct’. Then he mentioned similar to it’.
